title: Joiner edits relationship details and gets an unexplained failure
preconditions: A created the space; B joined as the partner.
B opens Account and chooses Edit relationship.
B changes the anniversary date and saves.

actions.note: B opens Edit relationship and saves a new date.

expected_behavior: A non-creator is either not offered the edit action or told plainly that only the creator can change space details.
A failed save explains the rule and preserves the current values.
The UI never implies that the partner's change was saved.
candidate_failure_modes: The partner taps a working-looking Edit relationship row, fills the form, and receives only "Unable to save. Please try again."
The partner retries because the message implies a transient network problem.
The partner believes the anniversary date changed when the server rejected it.

observed_code_behavior: Spaces enforce one active membership per user and one active partner per space at the storage layer.
Joining redeems an invite once; an expired or already-redeemed code is rejected, and a historical partner slot is permanently bound.
Leaving flips the caller's membership to left and keeps shared history for the remaining member.
Space hydration, foreground refresh, and mutation callbacks are scoped to the signed-in user id.
documented_requirement: A non-creator is either not offered the edit action or told plainly that only the creator can change space details.
A failed save explains the rule and preserves the current values.
The UI never implies that the partner's change was saved.
hypothetical_user_behavior: A fictional participant (Nadia Iqbal) said: "We are auditing Aoi for things that do not need to exist. Walk through the shared-memory flow you actually used this week: the composer, the Keep button, pending rows, retry and edit, author labels, the feed and gallery, empty and failed states, and every confirmation or helper line. For each one, ask out loud: "Why does this even exist?" Then say what would break if it were removed, and what it cost you. Name the three most useless things and the one thing you would keep. Do not propose a redesign; remove."

A fictional participant (Nadia Iqbal) said: "Ran this on my commute, one-handed, which is the honest test.

Three things that do not need to exist:

1. "Keep" as a separate verb from "Save." Two words for one state change means I have to guess which one is durable. What breaks if it's removed: nothing — the action still happens, I just stop pausing over it. Cost: a hesitation every single time, plus a nagging worry that Keep is a draft and Save is real.

2. Pending rows whose only feedback is a spinner. A spinner tells me time is passing, not what is happening or whether it will fail. What breaks if removed: nothing, provided there's a text state ("Saving…" → "Saved" → "Couldn't save. Retry"). Cost: I sit there refreshing to find out if I lost the thing.

3. Author labels on my own posts in the feed. I know it's me. What breaks if removed: nothing on my own rows. Cost: visual noise that pushes the actual content down, and it makes every card taller than the type inside it justifies.

The one I'd keep: retry and edit on a failed row. It's the only place in the flow where the interface admits something went wrong AND gives me a way out. That's not decoration, that's the state machine being visible.

Related, and it's the same failure mode: disabled buttons with no reason attached. If I can't tell why it's disabled, I'll assume the app is broken rather than that I'm missing a field. A one-line helper beats a tooltip — it shouldn't need hovering to explain itself."

A fictional participant (Theo Bennett) said: "Ran this literally, out loud, on a train with two bars of signal. Results:

1. The Keep button. Why does it exist? Because we don't trust the draft. But the draft is already in memory and already written to disk on every keystroke — Keep is a second save layered on the first. Remove it and nothing breaks: the text is still there after a rotation, after backgrounding, after a force-quit. What it costs: one tap, and worse, a doubt. Any flow where I press Keep and then have to check whether it kept has already lost. Delete it and make "saved" a state, not an action.

2. Author labels on pending rows in my own single-account memory flow. I am the only person here. At 200% text in split screen that label is the first thing to wrap and the thing that pushes the pending state off-screen — the only information on the row that matters. Remove it and nothing breaks. Cost: it actively hides the useful bit.

3. The post-retry helper line. It reads "Retrying…" with no timestamp, no attempt count, no distinction between "in flight" and "queued until you're online". On a patchy connection it just says "Retrying…" forever while the network is plainly gone. That's not a helper, that's the app lying about network state. Remove it, or replace it with the truth: "queued, will send when online." A status that cannot be false is the only status worth rendering.

Honourable mention, cut anyway: separate feed and gallery as two presentations of the same records, each with its own empty and failed state to keep in sync. Two chances to be wrong.

The one I would keep: the pending row itself. A visible, persistent row that survives rotation, backgrounding and refresh, that I can retry, and that I can edit in place without losing what I typed. That's the honest ledger of what has and hasn't left the device. Everything else is decoration on top of it.

Test I'd use to defend that decision: type a 400-word note, rotate, background for ten minutes, come back on a dead connection, edit the middle of it, refresh. If the pending row is the only thing that told me the truth the whole way through, it stays."
Nadia Iqbal assumes: a disabled button explains why
Nadia Iqbal assumes: a save has a visible pending and failure state
Theo Bennett assumes: a pending upload is visibly pending
Theo Bennett assumes: a six-character code accepts a pasted message
